Law and Justice (Polish: Prawo i Sprawiedliwość, PiS) is a right-wing populist and national-conservative political party in Poland.

Workers' Party of Korea: Kim Il-sung. Founded in 1949 from a merger between the Workers' Party of North Korea and the Workers' Party of South Korea, the WPK is the oldest active party in Korea.

2026 Asian Games: Japan. Nagoya will be the third Japanese city to host the Asian Games, after Tokyo in 1958 and Hiroshima in 1994.

Roman Republic: Latin. Its political organisation developed at around the same time as direct democracy in ancient Greece, with collective and annual magistracies, overseen by a senate.
Which of these was an official language of Joseon?
Joseon: Korean. It was founded by Taejo of Joseon in 1392 and replaced by the Korean Empire in 1897.

Kingdom of East Anglia: Old English. The kingdom formed in the 6th century in the wake of the Anglo-Saxon settlement of Britain was one of the kingdoms of the Heptarchy.
Which country used the assignat as its official currency?

The assignat is the official currency of French First Republic. The First Republic lasted until the declaration of the First Empire on 18 May 1804 under Napoléon Bonaparte, although the form of government changed several times.
Selected by NASA in 1963, this naval aviator and aeronautical engineer became the fourth person to walk on the Moon — and later traded the cockpit for the easel as a painter. Who was he?
Alan Bean (March 15, 1932 - May 26, 2018) was an American naval officer and aviator, aeronautical engineer, test pilot, NASA astronaut and painter.
United around 3150 BC by a ruler called Menes or Narmer, this Nile-valley civilization is considered one of the world's cradles of civilization — name it?
Ancient Egypt was a cradle of civilization concentrated along the lower reaches of the Nile River in the northeastern corner of Africa.
This Greek god of medicine, said to be a son of Apollo, had daughters named for concepts like Health and Recuperation, and represents the healing side of the ancient medical arts — who is he?
Asclepius (Ancient) is a hero and god of medicine in ancient Greek religion and mythology.
He was the principal organizer of the 1963 March on Washington and a leader for civil rights, socialism, nonviolence, and gay rights — which activist is it?
Bayard Rustin (March 17, 1912 - August 24, 1987) was an American political activist and prominent leader in social movements for civil rights, socialism, nonviolence, and gay rights.
This Turkish statesman and poet served as prime minister four separate times between 1974 and 2002, chairing first the Republican People's Party and later his own Democratic Left Party — who is he?
Bülent Ecevit (28 May 1925 - 5 November 2006) was a Turkish statesman, poet, writer, scholar, and journalist.

This Republican engineer, whose father once served as New Hampshire governor and White House chief of staff, was himself elected governor of that state four times, matching only one predecessor. Who is he?
Chris Sununu (s-; born November 5, 1974) is an American politician and engineer who served as the 82nd governor of New Hampshire from 2017 to 2025.

The U.S. Navy's first-ever rear admiral, vice admiral, and admiral is remembered for a bold order at the Battle of Mobile Bay usually shortened to 'Damn the torpedoes ... full speed ahead.' Who was he?
Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Viscount of Turenne
David Farragut (also spelled Glascoe; July 5, 1801 - August 14, 1870) was a flag officer of the United States Navy during the American Civil War.
This New Zealand mountaineer, alongside Tenzing Norgay, became the first climber confirmed to reach the summit of Mount Everest, on 29 May 1953 — who is he?
Edmund Hillary (20 July 1919 - 11 January 2008) was a New Zealand mountaineer, explorer, and philanthropist.
Once dubbed the 'Hop King of the World,' this Oregon Trail pioneer crossed the continent by ox-drawn wagon as a youth, then spent his later years retracing the route to memorialize it — who was he?
Robert Cecil, Viscount Cecil of Chelwood
Ezra Meeker (December 29, 1830 - December 3, 1928) was an American pioneer who traveled the Oregon Trail by ox-drawn wagon as a young man, migrating from Iowa to the Pacific Coast.

Waged by Julius Caesar between 58 and 50 BC against the tribes of Gaul, this decade of Roman military campaigns culminated in the Battle of Alesia and the Republic's total conquest of the region. What conflict is this?
Gallic Wars were waged between 58 and 50 BC by the Roman general Julius Caesar against the peoples of Gaul (present-day France, Belgium, and Switzerland).

This Russian mystic and faith healer gained enormous influence over the imperial family of Tsar Nicholas II in the final years of the empire. Born a Siberian peasant in 1869, he's best remembered for his mysterious sway over the fate of Russia itself — who is this controversial figure?
Grigori Rasputin was Russian mystic (1869–1916). Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin (21 January [O.S. 9 January] 1869 – 30 December [O.S. 17 December] 1916) was a Russian mystic and faith healer.
FDR's vice president from 1941 to 1945, this Iowa-born agriculture and commerce secretary later ran for the White House as the new Progressive Party's nominee in 1948 — who was he?
Henry A. Wallace (October 7, 1888 - November 18, 1965) was the 33rd vice president of the United States, serving from 1941 to 1945, under President Franklin D. Roosevelt.

A Scottish politician born to Pakistani immigrant parents became the youngest justice secretary in 2018, then health secretary, before leading his party and nation from March 2023 to May 2024. Who served as First Minister of Scotland?
Humza Yousaf (born 7 April 1985) is a Scottish politician who served as First Minister of Scotland and Leader of the Scottish National Party (SNP) from March 2023 to May 2024.
An anti-apartheid fighter who spent ten years on Robben Island, this man rose to lead the ANC and then served as South Africa's president from 2009 to 2018 — who is he?
Jacob Zuma (born 12 April 1942) is a South African politician who served as the president of South Africa from 2009 to 2018.

This West Virginia politician served as secretary of state, then governor, then US senator over a 24-year span, remaining a Democrat until switching to independent in 2024; he also co-founded a coal brokerage company. Who is he?
Joe Manchin (born August 24, 1947) is an American politician and businessman from West Virginia.
Succeeding Rowan Williams in 2013, this archbishop presided over the wedding of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle during a tenure that saw the church's first female bishop ordained — who is he?
Justin Welby (born 6 January 1956) is a retired Anglican bishop who served as the 105th archbishop of Canterbury in the Church of England from 2013 to 2025.
A former transplant surgeon nicknamed 'Ko P,' this Taiwanese politician served as mayor of Taipei before founding his own political party. Who is he?
Ko Wen-je (pinyin: K Wnzh; born 6 August 1959), also known by his nickname Ko P, is a Taiwanese politician, physician, and transplant surgeon who served as the 13th mayor of Taipei from 2014 to 2022.
Relieved from her post by the Secretary of Defense in 2025, this admiral had been the first woman to serve as chief of naval operations and the first woman on the Joint Chiefs of Staff — who is she?

Lisa Franchetti (fran-; born 25 April 1964) is a retired United States Navy admiral who served as the 33rd chief of naval operations from 2 November 2023 to 21 February 2025, after being relieved by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.
After representing Florida in the Senate for over a decade, this Republican politician became the nation's top diplomat and acting national security advisor in 2025 — who is he?
Marco Rubio (born May 28, 1971) is an American politician, attorney, and diplomat serving as the 72nd United States secretary of state since 2025.

Ruling the Franks from the mid-5th century until Pepin the Short's takeover in 751, this dynasty defeated the Visigoths in 507 and the Burgundians in 534 to build Western Europe's most powerful realm — which dynasty?
Merovingian dynasty was the ruling family of the Franks from around the middle of the 5th century until Pepin the Short in 751.

This Indian independence activist and politician served as prime minister from 1977 to 1979 leading the Janata Party government, after decades holding posts from Bombay's chief ministership to deputy prime minister — who is he?
Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence and Avondale

Morarji Desai (29 February 1896 - 10 April 1995) was an Indian politician and independence activist who served as the prime minister of India between 1977 and 1979 leading the government formed by the Janata Party.

This Florentine diplomat served Florence's republic while the Medici were out of power, then wrote a slim political treatise — unpublished until five years after his death — that earned him the title 'father of modern political science.' Who was he?
Niccolò Machiavelli (3 May 1469 - 21 June 1527) was a Florentine diplomat, author, philosopher, and historian who lived during the Italian Renaissance.
Backed by the Byzantine emperor Zeno, this Germanic people's king invaded Italy and preserved Roman law and administration from his capital at Ravenna — who were they?
Ostrogoths were a Roman-era Germanic people who, in the 5th and 6th centuries, established one of the two major Gothic kingdoms within the Western Roman Empire.
This former Dutch MP, who focused on tax and pension policy, stepped away from politics in 2025 citing burnout after founding the New Social Contract party — who is he?
Alfred, Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha

Pieter Omtzigt (born 8 January 1974) is a Dutch former politician who served as a member of the House of Representatives between 2003 and 2025 apart from a short interruption between June and October 2010.
Chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, this Kentucky Republican ran for his party's presidential nomination in 2016 — who is he?
Rand Paul (born January 7, 1963) is an American politician serving as the junior United States senator from Kentucky since 2011.

In 1941 this Deputy to the Führer made a bizarre solo flight to Scotland hoping to talk Britain out of the war — and ended up a prisoner, later dying by suicide at 93 while still serving a life sentence. Who was he?
Rudolf Hess (He in German; 26 April 1894 - 17 August 1987) was a German politician, convicted war criminal, and a leading member of the Nazi Party in Germany.
An Old Bolshevik and Politburo member who led the Communist Party in Leningrad, he was gunned down at his office in 1934 — an assassination Stalin used to launch the Great Purge. Who was he?
Sergei Kirov (born Kostrikov; 27 March 1886 - 1 December 1934) was a Russian and Soviet politician and Bolshevik revolutionary.
Founded by crusading knights along the Baltic during the 13th-century Northern Crusades, this theocratic realm at its peak stretched from Prussia to Estonia and included Gotland — what was it called?
State of the Teutonic Order was a theocratic state located along the southeastern shore of the Baltic Sea in northern Europe.

This ancient Indo-European-speaking people inhabited large parts of Southeast Europe, in territory spanning modern Bulgaria, Romania, and northern Greece, as well as parts of northwestern Anatolia — who were they?
Thracians were an Indo-European-speaking people who inhabited large parts of Southeast Europe in ancient history. The Thracian culture emerged during the early Bronze Age, which began about 3500 BC.
This Argentine lawyer and conservative politician has served as her country's vice president since 2023, having founded a legal-studies center focused on terrorism victims. Who is she?
Victoria Villarruel (born 13 April 1975) is an Argentine politician, lawyer, writer, and activist who has served as the 38th vice president of Argentina since 2023.

Co-founder of the Center for Constitutional Rights and defender of the Chicago Seven, this attorney was dubbed by The New York Times 'the country's most controversial and, perhaps, its best-known lawyer.' Who?
William Kunstler (July 7, 1919 - September 4, 1995) was an American attorney and civil rights activist, known for defending the Chicago Seven.
Centered on the Avesta and the teachings of an ancient Iranian prophet, this faith — among the world's oldest organized religions — reveres a supreme deity named Ahura Mazda — name the religion?
Zoroastrianism is an Iranian religion centred on the Avesta and the teachings of Zarathushtra Spitama, who is more commonly referred to by the Greek translation, Zoroaster (Ancient).
Traditionally chanted by a muezzin from a mosque's minaret before each of the five daily prayers, what is this Islamic call known as?
Adhan: Islamic call to prayer. The five prayer times are known in Arabic as fajr (فجر), dhuhr (ظهر), asr (عصر), maghrib (مغرب), and isha (عشاء).
A criminal-law professor who earned his law degree at 24, this Peronist served as Argentina's longest-tenured Cabinet Chief before becoming the country's president from 2019 to 2023 — who is he?

Alberto Fernández: President of Argentina from 2019 to 2023. Born in Buenos Aires, Fernández attended the University of Buenos Aires, where he earned his law degree at age 24, and later became a professor of criminal law.
In 2024, this Manhattan district attorney became the first person to secure a criminal conviction of a former U.S. president — who is he?
Alvin Bragg: American lawyer and politician (born 1973)
Educated in France and once slated to marry an Irish earl, she instead became Henry VIII's second wife — and was beheaded for treason in 1536. Who was she?
Anne Boleyn: Queen of England from 1533 to 1536.
This 656 CE killing of the third Rashidun caliph came after protesters-turned-rebels besieged his house and set it ablaze, sparking lasting debate over Islamic rulership — what event is this?
Assassination of Uthman: 656 murder of the third Rashidun caliph in Medina.

In 52 BC, Julius Caesar trapped Vercingetorix by building two rings of fortifications at once — an inner wall to pen the Gauls in and an outer wall to fend off their relief army. Which siege was this?
Battle of Alesia: Part of the Gallic Wars.
Born in the United States and raised in Switzerland, this monarch reigned for over 70 years — the longest of any Thai king — after his brother died mysteriously — who was he?
Bhumibol Adulyadej: King of Thailand from 1946 to 2016.
Serving as Turkey's prime minister four separate times between 1974 and 2002, he also invaded Cyprus and lifted a ban on opium cultivation during his first term — who is he?
Bülent Ecevit: Prime Minister of Turkey (1974; 1977; 1978–79; 1999–2002)
Serving since 2023, this politician is Turkey's second-ever vice president and previously ran the country's Ministry of Development — who is he?
Cevdet Yılmaz: Vice President of Turkey since 2023. Cevdet Yılmaz (born 1 April 1967) is a Turkish politician who has been the 2nd and current vice president of Turkey since 2023.
This South Korean general seized power after the 1979 assassination of the country's previous dictator, then declared martial law and became the nation's fifth president — who is he?
Chun Doo-hwan: Leader of South Korea from 1979 to 1988.

Formed in 1230 by the union of two Iberian kingdoms, this medieval polity was tied to Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage of discovery and endured until Philip V's 1716 reforms dissolved it. What was this realm called?
Crown of Castile: Former country in the Iberian Peninsula from 1230 to 1715.
The Olympian goddess of harvest and agriculture, she was swallowed by her father Cronus as an infant and later became the mother of Persephone by Zeus — who is she?
Demeter: Greek goddess of the harvest, grains, and agriculture.
Often depicted riding a lion or tiger with many arms, each wielding a weapon, this Hindu goddess embodies the triumph of good over evil — who is she?
The longest-serving U.S. first lady, she went on to help draft the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a UN delegate, earning a standing ovation when it was adopted — who was she?
Eleanor Roosevelt: American diplomat and activist (1884–1962)
A five-time Socialist Party candidate for U.S. president, this labor leader co-founded the Industrial Workers of the World and led a major railway strike against the CB&Q line in 1888. Who is he?
Eugene V. Debs: American labor and political leader (1855–1926)
It erupted in 1989 when Charles Taylor's NPFL invaded from Ivory Coast to topple President Samuel Doe, who was soon captured and executed by a splinter faction — which conflict is this?
First Liberian Civil War: 1989–1997 war in West Africa.
Dwelling in the wetland halls of Fensalir, this Norse goddess of marriage and prophecy was the wife of Odin — who is she?
Frigg: Germanic goddess. The names ultimately stem from the Proto-Germanic theonym *Frijjō.
This Roman general campaigned against Arminius in Germania, and his honorific title honored his father's own victories there before he was adopted by his uncle Tiberius. Who was he?
Sparked when Saddam Hussein's Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990 over an oil-field drilling dispute, this conflict pitted a 42-country coalition against him in Operation Desert Storm — what is it called?
Gulf War: 1990–1991 conflict in the Middle East.
Son of Cnut the Great, this ruler was the last monarch of the North Sea Empire uniting England and Denmark before dying suddenly in 1042 — who was he?
Harthacnut: King of England (1040–42) and Denmark (1035–42)
After 28 years in Soviet state security and a long reign as Azerbaijan's Communist Party boss, this man rose to become his country's third president in 1993 — who was he?
Heydar Aliyev: President of Azerbaijan from 1993 to 2003.
Left for dead by his companions after a grizzly mauling on the Upper Missouri, this frontiersman's survival inspired the films Man in the Wilderness and The Revenant — who was he?
Hugh Glass: American fur trapper and frontiersman (1783–1833)
In 1980, six gunmen demanding independence for a province of Iran stormed a London diplomatic compound, holding 26 hostages during a six-day standoff — which historic event?
Iranian Embassy siege: 1980 hostage situation in London.
The only surviving son of Emperor Akbar, this Mughal ruler was schooled in Chagatai, Persian and Hindustani before taking the throne and reigning from 1605 to 1627. Who is he?
Jahangir: Mughal emperor from 1605 to 1627. The third and only surviving son of Emperor Akbar I (r. 1556–1605) and his consort Maryam uz-Zamani.

A WWII Marine flying ace awarded the Navy Cross over Okinawa, this Mississippi politician later served as mayor of Biloxi and won a $500 million jury verdict against a rival funeral-home company — who is he?

Jeremiah Joseph O'Keefe: American politician. Jeremiah Joseph O'Keefe III (July 12, 1923 – August 23, 2016) was an American fighter ace, Democratic Party politician, insurance executive, and funeral director.

Elected vice president on the 1840 Whig ticket, this man became the tenth U.S. president just 31 days into his running mate's term after his sudden death — leaving him estranged from both major parties. Who was he?
John Tyler: President of the United States from 1841 to 1845.
After an 11-year career in the oil industry, this 105th Archbishop of Canterbury officiated the coronation of Charles III and the state funeral of Elizabeth II — who is he?
Justin Welby: Archbishop of Canterbury from 2013 to 2025.
As Abu Dhabi's ruler from 2004, this leader helped bring the Louvre, a New York University campus, and Etihad Airways to the emirate — who was he?
Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan: President of the United Arab Emirates from 2004 to 2022.

Medically retired from the Marines, this Medal of Honor recipient earned the nation's highest military honor for actions in Afghanistan's Helmand Province in 2010, making him the youngest living recipient — who is he?

Serving the state of Zhao during the Warring States period, this general — one of Chinese folklore's 'Four Greatest Generals' — died in 229 BC and is remembered as a master of defensive tactics. Who was he?
This Texan went from teacher to congressional aide to the U.S. House, then ascended from the vice presidency to the White House in 1963 after a president's assassination — who was he?
Lyndon B. Johnson: President of the United States from 1963 to 1969.
A billionaire Emirati royal and brother of the UAE's president, this sheikh holds stakes in football clubs around the world through the City Football Group — who is he?
Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan: Vice President of the United Arab Emirates.
Raised an Anglican though her parents had converted to Catholicism, this English queen ruled jointly with her husband — their reign remembered simply as "William and ___." Who was she?
Mary II: Queen of England, Scotland, and Ireland from 1689 to 1694.
The longest-serving governor in Massachusetts history, this Democrat lost the 1988 presidential election to George H. W. Bush — who is he?
Michael Dukakis: American politician and lawyer (born 1933)
Once considered one of the finest ODI batsmen in the world, this Indian captain led three World Cup campaigns in the 1990s before a life ban for match-fixing ended his career — who is he?

Mohammad Azharuddin: Indian cricketer. Mohammad Azizuddin Azharuddin (born 8 February 1963) is an Indian politician and a former cricketer who also served as the Indian national cricket team's captain.
A former footballer and journalist before entering politics, this BJP leader served as the 12th Chief Minister of Manipur from 2017 to 2025 — who is he?
N. Biren Singh: Chief Minister of Manipur from 2017 to 2025. Joining politics in 2002, Biren joined the Democratic Revolutionary Peoples Party and won the assembly elections from Heingang.
A onetime metal worker who rose through Soviet ranks under Lazar Kaganovich, this leader shocked the world by denouncing Stalin and presided over the Cuban Missile Crisis — who was he?
Nikita Khrushchev: Leader of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964.

A boilermaker before West Point, this U.S. general graduated in 1915 alongside Dwight Eisenhower in "the class the stars fell on" and later became the first chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff — who is he?
Omar Bradley: United States Army general (1893–1981)

Born to a Tutsi family that fled to Uganda when he was two, this politician commanded a rebel force that ended the 1994 genocide in his home country and has served as its president since 2000 — who is he?
Paul Kagame: President of Rwanda since 2000. The RPF was one of the main belligerents of the Rwandan Civil War and was the armed force which ended the 1994 Rwandan genocide.
Educated in New Zealand and the United States, this Thai businessman led the Move Forward Party, successor to the dissolved Future Forward Party — who is he?
Pita Limjaroenrat: Thai businessman and politician (born 1980)

Known as Bilqis in Arabic and Makeda in Ge'ez, this Hebrew Bible figure brought a caravan of lavish gifts to King Solomon and is linked by modern historians to an ancient South Arabian kingdom in Yemen?
Queen of Sheba: Historical figure in the Abrahamic religions.
Widely considered the greatest mountaineer ever, who made the first solo ascent of Everest and was the first to climb all fourteen eight-thousanders without supplemental oxygen?
Reinhold Messner: Italian mountaineer, adventurer and explorer (born 1944)

Born when Octavian rose to power and established the Augustan Principate in 27 BC, its western half fell in 476 AD while its eastern half lived on until Constantinople fell in 1453. What state is this?
Roman Empire: 27 BC–476/1453 AD state and civilization. The Roman Empire was a state that dominated the Mediterranean and much of Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa during the classical period.

In 1982 this child from Manchester, Maine wrote a letter to Soviet leader Yuri Andropov — and got a personal reply inviting her to visit the USSR, making her 'America's Youngest Ambassador' — who was she?
Samantha Smith: American child peace activist (1972–1985)
Nicknamed "the Grim," this Ottoman sultan grew his empire by seventy percent in just eight years, conquering the entire Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt between 1516 and 1517 — who was he?
Selim I: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1512 to 1520.
After a 1969 coup, this army commander became Somalia's third president and reconstituted the country as a one-party Marxist-Leninist state — who is he?
Siad Barre: President of Somalia from 1969 to 1991.

Defined by a one-man police state, forced agricultural collectivization, and a sweeping cult of personality, this set of Soviet policies held sway from 1927 until the dictator's death in 1953 — what is it called?
Stalinism: Political and economic policies implemented by Joseph Stalin.
Led by a man who declared himself the younger brother of Jesus Christ, this 1850s Chinese theocratic state waged a 14-year war against the Qing dynasty — what was it?
Taiping Heavenly Kingdom: Theocratic monarchy in China (1851–1864)
A Whig historian famed for his prose, he both wrote a seminal "History of England" and played a major role in shaping India's education policy — who was he?
Thomas Babington Macaulay: British historian and politician (1800–1859)

Serving as the eighth U.S. director of national intelligence starting in 2025, this former Hawaii congresswoman deployed to Iraq with the National Guard and later left the Democrats to become a Republican — who is she?
Tulsi Gabbard: American politician and military officer (born 1981)

Set to become just the fourth queen to rule her Scandinavian kingdom in her own right — and the first since 1720 — she is heir apparent thanks to a 1980 law that was Western Europe's first with absolute primogeniture. Who is she?
Victoria, Crown Princess of Sweden: Heir apparent to the Swedish throne (born 1977)
Fought along the Suez Canal from 1967 to 1970 after Arab leaders adopted the 'three no's' policy, this conflict pitted Israel against Egypt, Jordan, and the PLO?
War of Attrition: 1967–1970 war between Israel and Egypt. Following the 1967 Six-Day War, no serious diplomatic efforts were made to resolve the issues at the heart of the Arab–Israeli conflict.
It's the season that arrives when your hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, so that while one half of Earth shivers the other basks in summer. Which season?
Winter: Coldest of the four temperate seasons.
This Japanese samurai, who lived from 1574 to 1607, served as daimyō of the Fukui Domain in Echizen during the transition into the Edo period — who is he?
Yūki Hideyasu: Japanese samurai. Yūki Hideyasu (結城 秀康; 1 March 1574 – 2 June 1607) was a Japanese samurai who lived during the Azuchi–Momoyama and early Edo periods.
Which of these people was born first?
Thomas Carlyle (born 1795) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
SQL (founded 1974) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these was founded earliest?
C (programming language) (founded 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Maria Goeppert Mayer is a physicist. In 1986, the Maria Goeppert Mayer Award for early-career women physicists was established in her honor.
Who among these is a chemist?
Ivan Pavlov is a chemist. Pavlov also conducted significant research on the physiology of digestion, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1904.
What is the atomic number of Neodymium?
Neodymium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nd and atomic number 60.
In what year was Hamish Harding born?
Hamish Harding: George Hamish Livingston Harding (24 June 1964 – 18 June 2023) was a British businessman, pilot and adventurer based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
In what year did Aristotle die?
Aristotle (Ancient Greek: Ἀριστοτέλης, romanized: Aristotélēs; 384–322 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath.
In what year was Phosphorus discovered?
Phosphorus is a chemical element; it has symbol P and atomic number 15.

Sukhoi Su-57: Komsomolsk-on-Amur Aircraft Production Association. The Sukhoi Su-57 (Russian: Сухой Су-57; NATO reporting name: Felon) is a twin-engine stealth multirole fighter aircraft developed by Sukhoi.
In which country did the Hawker Hurricane take place?
Hawker Hurricane: United Kingdom. The Air Ministry ordered Hawker's Interceptor Monoplane in late 1934, and the prototype Hurricane K5083 performed its maiden flight on 6 November 1935.
Who is credited with discovering Norma?

Norma (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is Latin for normal, referring to a right angle, and is variously considered to represent a rule, a carpenter's square, a set square or a level.
Who is credited with discovering Aspartame?
Aspartame: James M. Schlatter. Aspartame is an artificial, non-saccharide sweetener commonly used as a sugar substitute in foods and beverages.
Who is credited with discovering Histamine?
Histamine: Henry Hallett Dale. Histamine or histamin is an organic nitrogenous compound found in mammals and many vegetables, fruits and food products.
About 5 million tonnes of acetic acid are produced annually largely to make this compound, most commonly in polymer form — what is it?
Acetate is a salt formed by the combination of acetic acid with a base (e.g. sodium hydroxide), an ester of acetic acid, or the anion CH3COO- found in solution.

Native to South America but cultivated in Europe since the 17th century for its fragrant oil, this flowering member of the verbena family is better known by a common name referencing a citrus fruit — what's its scientific name?
Aloysia citrodora is a species of flowering plant in the verbena family Verbenaceae, native to South America.
This scientific discipline bridges biology and sociology, studying human behavior, cultures, societies, and languages across time. What field is it?

Anthropology is the scientific study of humanity that crosses biology and sociology, concerned with human behavior, human biology, cultures, societies, and linguistics, in both the present and past, including archaic humans.

It's one of the oldest natural sciences, recruiting math, physics, and chemistry to explain everything that originates beyond Earth's atmosphere — from comets and quasars to the cosmic microwave background. What field is it?
Astronomy is a natural science that studies celestial objects and the phenomena that occur in the cosmos.
This perennial flowering plant species, native to Eurasia and growing up to four feet tall, includes cultivated varieties used for sugar, its edible root, and its edible leaves — what species is it?
Beta vulgaris (beet) is a species of flowering plant in the subfamily Betoideae of the family Amaranthaceae.
Members of this decapod infraorder tuck a tiny tail-like abdomen under a hard thorax and end their front legs in pincers — which true creatures are they?
Brachyura is an infraorder of decapod crustaceans comprising the true crabs.
This opportunistic yeast lives harmlessly in the gut and mouth of most healthy adults, but can turn pathogenic in immunocompromised people, causing a common fungal infection — what species is it?
Candida albicans is an opportunistic pathogenic yeast that is a common member of the human gut flora.
Famous for color-shifting camouflage and zygodactylous, pincer-like feet, which family of roughly 200 Old World lizard species is this?
Chameleon (family Chamaeleonidae) are a distinctive and highly specialized clade of Old World lizards with 200 species described as of June 2015.

Largely self-taught and grinding his own lenses from spare parts on a Kansas farm, this astronomer's homemade skills landed him at Lowell Observatory — where his 1930 survey turned up the first known body in the Kuiper belt; who was he?

Clyde Tombaugh (February 4, 1906 - January 17, 1997) was an American astronomer and telescope maker, best known for discovering Pluto in 1930, marking the first detection of what would eventually be recognized as the Kuiper belt.
Derived from Greek words meaning universe and study of, this scientific and philosophical field examines the nature of existence at the grandest scale — what is it called?
Cosmology (from Ancient Greek (cosmos) 'the universe, the world' and - (logia) 'study of') is the study of the nature of the universe, the cosmos.
This Asian canid stands apart from true dogs: a convex rather than concave skull, no third lower molar, and single-cusped upper molars — once it roamed into Europe. What is it?
Dhole (dohl; Cuon alpinus) is a canid native to South, East and Southeast Asia.
Which natural science examines how living things relate to their environment, spanning the individual, population, community, ecosystem, and biosphere levels?
Ecology (from Ancient Greek (okos) 'house' and - (-loga) 'study of') is the natural science of the relationships among living organisms and their environment.

This Austrian physicist devised a foundational equation for calculating a quantum system's wave function and coined the term 'quantum entanglement,' sharing the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac — who is he?
Erwin Schrödinger (12 August 1887 - 4 January 1961), sometimes written as Schroedinger or Schrodinger, was an Austrian theoretical physicist who developed fundamental results in quantum theory.

This Arabic term describes the human interpretation and practice of Islamic religious law, expanded through jurists' scholarly reasoning and expressed in the rulings they issue on questions of faith. What is this field called?
Fiqh is the term for Islamic jurisprudence. Thus, whereas sharia is considered immutable and infallible by Muslims, fiqh is considered fallible and changeable.
Practitioners of this discipline monitor crustal motion, tides, and polar shifts to maintain accurate global positioning reference frames — what is this field called?
Geodesy (jee-) or geodetics is the science of measuring and representing the geometry, gravity, and spatial orientation of the Earth in temporally varying 3D space.
Endemic to Africa and among the oldest of the gallinaceous birds, this family branched off before New World quail evolutionarily — name the birds?
Guinea fowl are birds of the family Numididae in the order Galliformes.
Planted for land reclamation thanks to its nitrogen-fixing, erosion-resisting root system, this deciduous shrub genus's berries also show up in human and animal food products — what genus is it?
Hippophae is a genus of flowering plants in the family Elaeagnaceae.

Once diagnosed almost exclusively in women as a physical illness in the 19th century, this term for ungovernable emotional excess later became the focus of research by Freud and Charcot — what is this condition called?
Hysteria is a term used to mean ungovernable emotional excess and can refer to a temporary state of mind or emotion.

This American economist gave his name to a model for censored dependent variables — the 'tobit' — and advised the Council of Economic Advisers while championing government action to head off recessions. Who was he?

James Tobin (March 5, 1918 - March 11, 2002) was an American economist who served on the Council of Economic Advisers and consulted with the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, and taught at Yale University.
A founder of modern geometric analysis, this American mathematician won the 2019 Abel Prize for pioneering work in geometric PDEs and gauge theory — who is she?
Karen Uhlenbeck (born August 24, 1942) is an American mathematician and one of the founders of modern geometric analysis.

A Cornell-trained engineer and Atlanta factory superintendent, this man was wrongly convicted of a young employee's murder, then kidnapped from prison and lynched in a case now central to American antisemitism — who was he?

Leo Frank (April 17, 1884 - August 17, 1915) was an American lynching victim wrongly convicted of the murder of 13-year-old Mary Phagan, an employee in a factory in Atlanta, Georgia, where he was the superintendent.
Born in Winnipeg and trained at King's College London, this physicist and chemist joined the Manhattan Project in 1942 to conduct experiments with uranium — who is he?
Louis Slotin (1 December 1910 - 30 May 1946) was a Canadian physicist and chemist who took part in the Manhattan Project.
He helped uncover the Antarctic ozone hole and shared a 1995 Nobel for exposing the danger CFCs pose to the ozone layer — which Mexican chemist?
Mario Molina (19 March 1943 - 7 October 2020) was a Mexican physical chemist.
Connecting the diencephalon and cerebrum to the pons, this brainstem structure plays a role in vision, hearing, and staying alert -- what is it called?
Midbrain is the uppermost portion of the brainstem connecting the diencephalon and cerebrum with the pons.

Chemically known as bis(2-chloroethyl) sulfide, this organosulfur compound is a potent alkylating agent and carcinogen with no preventive antidote — protection relies entirely on covering the skin and airways. Name this notorious chemical warfare agent?
Mustard gas are names commonly used for the organosulfur chemical compound bis(2-chloroethyl) sulfide, which has the chemical structure S(CH2CH2Cl)2, as well as other species.
Element 102 honors the inventor of dynamite, and its short-lived isotope 255 — with a 3-minute half-life — is the one chemists actually prefer to work with. Which synthetic actinide is it?
Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol No and atomic number 102.
Dubbed the father of nuclear chemistry, he studied under Ernest Rutherford before helping identify the radioactive elements radium, thorium, and protactinium — who is he?
Otto Hahn (8 March 1879 - 28 July 1968) was a German chemist who was a pioneer in the field of radiochemistry.
Listed in the Dictionary of Fungi as containing over 300 species, this mold genus produces a compound that stops bacterial growth and also flavors certain cheeses — which genus?
Penicillium is a genus of ascomycetous fungi that is part of the mycobiome of many species and is of major importance in the natural environment, in food spoilage, and in food and drug production.
Equal to one-eighth of a gallon in both the imperial and US customary systems, this unit of volume is just over 20% larger in Britain than it is in America — name it?
Pint (symbol pt, sometimes abbreviated as p) is a unit of volume or capacity in both the imperial and United States customary measurement systems.
Originating on Gran Canaria and Tenerife, this large Spanish mastiff-type breed was traditionally used to guard property, herd livestock, and, legally until 1936, fight other dogs — what breed is it?
Presa Canario is a Spanish breed of large dog of mastiff or catch dog type.
It can form not just from rain but from mist, spray, or dew, and though we usually see an arc, it can actually be a full circle — what optical phenomenon is it?
Rainbow is an optical phenomenon caused by refraction, internal reflection and dispersion of light in water droplets resulting in a continuous spectrum of light appearing in the sky.
Named for its type genus, this plant family of nearly 4,800 species includes the trees and shrubs behind apples, pears, plums, cherries, and peaches — what family is it?
Rosaceae is a family of flowering plants that includes 4,828 known species in 91 genera.
This synthetic element, atomic number 106, is so fleeting that only a few atoms exist at a time and decay within minutes — and it's named for an American nuclear chemist; what is it?
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Sg and atomic number 106.
Doctors recommend covering your elbow rather than your hands to block this involuntary, explosive rush of air from spreading illness through the air. What is this reflex called?
Sneeze (also known as sternutation) is a semi-autonomous, convulsive expulsion of air from the lungs through the nose and mouth, usually caused by foreign particles irritating the nasal mucosa.
This muscular, hollow organ in the upper digestive tract handles the gastric phase of digestion, and gives us the medical prefix 'gastric' from its Ancient Greek name — name the organ?
Stomach is a muscular, hollow organ in the upper gastrointestinal tract of humans and many other animals, including several invertebrates.
Sporting beaded antennae and a pale, soft-bodied worker caste, these decaying-wood eaters belong to the order Isoptera and are really highly derived cockroaches — what are they?
Termite are a group of eusocial insects which consume a variety of decaying plant material, generally in the form of wood, leaf litter, and soil humus.

Caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii and often spread through undercooked meat or contact with infected cat feces, this disease can be especially dangerous to a developing baby if a woman is infected during pregnancy — what is it?
Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic disease caused by Toxoplasma gondii, an apicomplexan.
This type of blood vessel usually carries deoxygenated blood toward the heart — except in the pulmonary and fetal circulation, where it carries oxygen-rich blood instead — what is it?
Vein is a blood vessel in the circulatory system of humans and most other animals that carries blood towards the heart.
This noble gas, found in trace amounts in Earth's atmosphere, powers arc lamps, serves as a rare anesthetic, and was the first of its family coaxed into a genuine chemical compound — which element?
Xenon is a chemical element; it has symbol Xe and atomic number 54.
Named for the skull-shaped marking on its thorax and first classified by Carl Linnaeus in 1758, this large moth was immortalized on the poster for 'The Silence of the Lambs' — which insect?
Acherontia atropos: Species of moth. It is most commonly identified by the vaguely skull-shaped pattern adorning the thorax, the characteristic from which its common and scientific names are derived.
Scientifically named Gadus chalcogrammus, this schooling member of the cod family gathers in massive numbers in the eastern Bering Sea — which fish?
Alaska pollock: Species of fish. The Alaska pollock also known as Pacific pollock or walleye pollock (Gadus chalcogrammus) is a marine fish species of the cod genus Gadus and family Gadidae.
Native to the Americas, this plant is better known by its common names common ragweed, annual ragweed, or low ragweed — what is its scientific name?
Ambrosia artemisiifolia: Species of flowering plant in the daisy family.

Named from Greek words meaning "unlike other shrimp," this extinct arthropod from the Burgess Shale had swimming flaps, big compound eyes and grasping frontal appendages, reaching over a foot long — which prehistoric predator?
Anomalocaris: Extinct genus of cambrian radiodont.

Nicknamed for its resemblance to a stinging insect, this orb-weaver spider sports bold yellow, white, and black bands across Central and Northern Europe, parts of Asia and Africa, and even the Azores — what species is it?
Argiope bruennichi: Species of orb-weaver spider. Like many other members of the same genus Argiope, this species has distinctive yellow, white and black markings on its abdomen.
Native to tropical Southeast Asia, this small tree bears bell-shaped rose-to-purple flowers and a ridged fruit that forms star-shaped slices when cut crosswise — which species?
Averrhoa carambola: Species of tree. It is a small tree or shrub that grows 5 to 12 m (16 to 39 ft) tall, with rose to red-purple flowers.

When no one else had the staff for it, this American lawyer volunteered to prosecute the Einsatzgruppen trial at Nuremberg, then spent decades championing an International Criminal Court — who was he?

In this distributed ledger, each record holds a cryptographic hash of the one before it, so altering a single block would require rewriting every block that follows — making the data nearly tamper-proof. What is it?
Blockchain: Distributed data store for digital transactions.
This plant family — nicknamed the mustards or crucifers, and including cabbage — hosts the caterpillars of a notorious garden-pest butterfly as one of its worst enemies — name the family?

Ranging from the hefty black species of the Amazon basin to the diminutive dwarf species just over a metre long, these Central and South American relatives of alligators make up their own reptile subfamily — what are they called?
Caiman: Subfamily of reptiles. The black caiman is the largest caiman species in the world and is found in the slow-moving rivers and lakes that surround the Amazon basin.

Born in London, raised in Milan, and self-taught in web design, this Catholic teenager built a website cataloguing Eucharistic miracles before dying of leukemia at fifteen — he was beatified in 2020. Who was he?
Which second-generation antihistamine for hay fever kicks in within half an hour but is more likely than fexofenadine or loratadine to cause drowsiness?

Cetirizine: Antihistamine medication. Cetirizine is a second-generation peripherally selective antihistamine used to treat allergic rhinitis (hay fever), dermatitis, urticaria (hives), and runny nose.
With about 3,400 species in over 520 genera, this insect family includes nearly every member of its group except two species in a small sister taxon — which family?
Used to treat gout, familial Mediterranean fever, and pericarditis, this medication has such a narrow therapeutic index that its injectable form was pulled from the US market in 2008. What is it?
Colchicine: Medication mainly used to treat gout. The American College of Rheumatology recommends colchicine, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or steroids in the treatment of gout.
Home to crows, ravens, magpies, and jays, this bird family boasts a brain-to-body ratio rivaling great apes, and one of its members even passed the mirror self-recognition test — what family is this?

A Scottish biologist, classicist and mathematician who pioneered theoretical biology, he's remembered for his 1917 book On Growth and Form, which opened the way to explaining how patterns and body structures take shape — who was he?
D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson: Scottish biologist, mathematician, and classics scholar.

This group of microalgae generates roughly a fifth to a half of Earth's oxygen each year, and its dead shells drift on Saharan winds to fertilize the entire Amazon basin with millions of tons of dust annually. What are they?
Diatom: Single-celled alga with a silica cell wall.
The only living relative of the extinct Steller's sea cow, this seagrass-grazing marine mammal is most abundant in the waters of northern Australia — what is it?
Dugong: Species of marine mammal. It is one of four living species of the order Sirenia, which also includes three species of manatees.
Co-founding Mattel with his wife Ruth, this inventor helped bring Barbie, Hot Wheels, and Chatty Cathy to toy shelves — who is he?
Elliot Handler: American inventor and business magnate (1916–2011)
Made by yeast fermenting sugars and once used as a general anesthetic, this colorless flammable liquid is the world's second most consumed drug, behind only caffeine — what is it?
Proposed in 1724 by a physicist who set water's freezing point at 32 degrees and boiling at 212, this temperature scale was originally anchored to a freezing brine solution — which scale?
Fahrenheit: Temperature scale. The Fahrenheit scale is a temperature scale based on one proposed in 1724 by the physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit (1686–1736).
Grown for both food and fiber, this plant's seeds are pressed into linseed oil while its stem fibers are woven into linen for sheets and clothing. What plant is it?
This Canadian physician and author has written five books linking childhood trauma to conditions like ADHD and addiction, though critics question the evidence behind some claims — who is he?
Caused by a genetic variant in the UGT1A1 gene, this harmless liver condition slows the breakdown of bilirubin and can trigger jaundice during stress, exercise, or fasting — what is it called?
Gilbert's syndrome: Medical condition. It is typically inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern and occasionally in an autosomal dominant pattern depending on the type of variant.

Despite its name, this marine reptile's shell ranges from olive to black — its nickname actually comes from the color of the fat beneath its carapace, built up from an all-plant diet — which species is this?
Green sea turtle: Species of large sea reptile. The dorsoventrally flattened body of C. mydas is covered by a large, teardrop-shaped carapace; it has a pair of large, paddle-like flippers.

Made by fusing heavy nuclei in tiny quantities, this superheavy element 108 has a special isotope whose "magic numbers" of protons and neutrons make its deformed nucleus unusually stable — what is it?
Hassium: Chemical element with atomic number 108 (Hs)
Its name means 'river horse' in Ancient Greek, yet this semiaquatic sub-Saharan giant — the largest even-toed ungulate alive — is more closely tied to pigs than to horses; what is it?
Hippopotamus: Species of large semi-aquatic mammal.
Marketed as Buscopan, this anticholinergic medication treats abdominal cramps, bladder and biliary spasms, and can ease respiratory secretions near the end of life — what drug is it?
Hyoscine butylbromide: Anticholinergic medication. It is also used to improve excessive respiratory secretions at the end of life.
Sitting on the electromagnetic spectrum between visible light and microwaves, this invisible radiation makes up most of the black-body glow given off by objects near room temperature — what is it?

Infrared: Form of electromagnetic radiation. Infrared (IR; sometimes called infrared light) is electromagnetic radiation (EMR) with wavelengths longer than that of visible light but shorter than microwaves.

This Dutch microscopist showed that an insect's egg, larva, pupa, and adult are all one animal, pioneered the microscope in dissections, and in 1658 became the first to observe red blood cells — who was he?
Jan Swammerdam: Dutch biologist and microscopist (1637–1680)
Committed to accuracy and verification, this occupation and set of methods involves gathering and distributing the day's news — what field is it?
Journalism: Production of reports on current events.
This colorless noble gas defined the length of the metre from 1960 to 1983, based on the wavelength of one of its spectral lines — which element?
Krypton: Chemical element with atomic number 36 (Kr)

Originally cultivated by the ancient Egyptians and now grown worldwide with China producing over half the crop, this leafy Asteraceae vegetable also has a stem-focused variety called celtuce — name the vegetable?
Lettuce: Species of annual plant of the daisy family, most often grown as a leaf vegetable.
Also called dragon's eye, this tropical fruit tree from the soapberry family produces fruit similar to lychee but with a milder aroma, and is native to Southeast Asia and southern China — what is it?
Longan: Species of tropical fruit-bearing tree.
Transmitted through the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes and caused by single-celled Plasmodium parasites, which disease's symptoms typically begin 10 to 15 days after infection?

Selected in 1969 as a dedicated air-superiority fighter and first flown in 1972, this twin-engine American jet boasts a staggering combat record of 106 victories and zero losses — which aircraft is it?
McDonnell Douglas F-15 Eagle: Multirole and air superiority fighter family.
Sold as Flagyl, this antibiotic and antiprotozoal fights everything from giardiasis to trichomoniasis — but it's notorious for leaving a metallic taste in your mouth — what is it?
Metronidazole: Antibiotic and antiprotozoal medication. Metronidazole, sold under the brand name Flagyl and Metrogyl among others, is an antibiotic and antiprotozoal medication.
Nicknamed 'water warts,' this viral skin infection causes small pink bumps with a telltale dimple in the center and usually clears up on its own within a year — what is it?

Molluscum contagiosum: Viral infection of the skin. Molluscum contagiosum (MC), sometimes called water warts, is a viral infection of the skin that results in small raised pink lesions with a dimple in the center.
In this group of bone-marrow cancers, blood cells fail to mature into healthy ones, and some cases progress into acute myeloid leukemia — what is it called?
Myelodysplastic syndrome: Diverse collection of blood-related cancers.
Unlike its niacin cousin, this form of vitamin B3 treats pellagra without causing skin flushing, and as a cream is used to fade acne scars and reduce hyperpigmentation — what is it?

Symbolized by the Greek letter omega, this SI unit of electrical resistance was named after a 19th-century German physicist and, since 2019, is defined as an exact value based on fundamental constants — what unit is it?
Ohm: SI derived unit of electrical resistance. The ohm (symbol: Ω, the uppercase Greek letter omega) is the unit of electrical resistance in the International System of Units (SI).
Sold in extended-release form under the brand name OxyContin, this highly addictive semi-synthetic opioid treats moderate to severe pain and brings relief within about fifteen minutes. What is it?
Oxycodone: Opioid medication. It is usually taken orally, and is available in immediate-release and controlled-release formulations.
Prized wood from this fruit tree's genus, Pyrus, is a favorite material for making high-quality woodwind instruments, and China grows about three-quarters of the world's crop — which fruit?
Pear: Edible fruits from the genus Pyrus.

First described by Carl Ludwig Koch in 1850, this family of over 2,000 araneomorph spiders includes the "cellar spider" and "vibrating spider" — and shares a famous leggy nickname with harvestmen and crane flies. What family is it?
Pholcidae: Family of spiders. The family, first described by Carl Ludwig Koch in 1850, is divided into 94 genera.
Sometimes called a 'collapsed lung,' this condition involves air trapped in the space between the lung and chest wall, causing sudden sharp one-sided chest pain — what is it?
Pneumothorax: Abnormal collection of air in the pleural space.
This beta blocker treats high blood pressure and performance anxiety alike, and can even shrink capillary hemangiomas in infants — what drug?
Propranolol: Beta blocker drug. It can be taken orally, rectally, or by intravenous injection.
First identified in the 1950s as a radio source, this extremely luminous galactic nucleus can outshine an entire galaxy like the Milky Way thousands of times over — what is it?
Quasar: Active galactic nucleus (AGN) containing a supermassive black hole.
Often compared to the film in a camera, this innermost, light-sensitive layer of the eye sends signals along the optic nerve to the visual cortex — what is it?
Retina: Part of the eye. The retina (from Latin rete 'net'; pl. retinae or retinas) is the innermost, light-sensitive layer of tissue of the eye.
Discovered in 1973 by Ruth Bishop via electron micrograph images, this fecal-oral pathogen is the leading cause of diarrheal illness in infants worldwide — which pathogen?
Rotavirus: Specific genus of RNA viruses.

Discovered in 1879 via spectral analysis of Scandinavian minerals, this silvery-white rare-earth element with atomic number 21 wasn't isolated in metallic form until 1937, and today it's prized for strengthening aluminum alloys — which element?
Scandium: Chemical element with atomic number 21 (Sc)
An adult female of this ruminant is a ewe, a castrated male a wether, and a young one a lamb — and with about 1.2 billion of them, they're easily the most common of their kind. What animal?
Sheep: Domesticated ruminant bred for meat, wool, and milk.
Nicknamed a 'truth serum' in popular culture despite dubious real-world reliability, this fast-acting barbiturate anesthetic is marketed under the brand name Pentothal — which drug?
Sodium thiopental: Barbiturate general anesthetic. It is the thiobarbiturate analog of pentobarbital, and an analog of thiobarbital.

An English dyer and astronomer, he was the first to systematically show, around 1729, that electricity could travel through metals — flipping the era's focus from mere static sparks to conduction. Who was he?
Stephen Gray (scientist): English physicist. Stephen Gray (December 1666 – February 1736) was an English dyer and astronomer who was the first to systematically experiment with electrical conduction.
Commonly known as fainting, this fast-onset, short-duration loss of consciousness and muscle strength is typically caused by a sudden drop in blood flow to the brain — what's the medical term?
Syncope (medicine): Transient loss of consciousness and postural tone.
Also sold under the name dronabinol, this principal psychoactive compound in cannabis is prescribed to relieve chemotherapy-induced nausea and HIV/AIDS-related appetite loss — what is it?
Tetrahydrocannabinol: Psychoactive component of cannabis. It is the principal psychoactive constituent of Cannabis and one of at least 113 total cannabinoids identified on the plant.
Sitting between cells and organs in the body's organization, this assembly of similar cells and their extracellular matrix takes its English name from a French word meaning 'to weave' — what is it?
Tissue (biology): Group of similar cells performing a specific function.
Roughly three times stiffer than steel and nearly as hard as diamond, this gray powder is sintered into cutting tools, armor-piercing bullets, and jewelry — what compound is it?
Tungsten carbide: Hard, dense and stiff chemical compound.
Unlike arteries, most of these thin-walled blood vessels carry deoxygenated blood back toward the heart — what are they?
Vein: Blood vessels that carry blood towards the heart.
A slow-moving filter-feeder and the largest known fish alive — the biggest reliably recorded stretched nearly 19 metres — this is the only living member of its family. What is it?
Whale shark: Largest living species of fish. The whale shark (Rhincodon typus) is a slow-moving, filter-feeding carpet shark and the largest known extant fish species.
These striped African equines share their genus with horses and asses, and the leading theory says their patterns evolved mainly to deter biting flies — what are they?
Zebra: Striped animal in the equid family.
What is the chemical symbol for bohrium?
The symbol for bohrium is Bh. Bohrium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Bh and atomic number 107.
The symbol for neon is Ne. Neon is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ne and the atomic number 10.
